title: Medium exam 8
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace a few steps: scripts and the current directory, group lists, systemd, archives, line continuation, uniq, pipelines, loops, mount points and expansion order.

questions.title: cd inside a script
questions.text: `s.sh` is executable and its only line is `cd /tmp`. From `/home/ana` you run `./s.sh` and then `pwd`. What does `pwd` print?

options.t: `/home/ana`
options.why: The script runs in a child shell; `cd` changes the directory of that shell, which ends with the script.

options.t: `/tmp`
options.why: The directory of a process is not shared with its parent: the change is lost when the script ends.

options.t: `/tmp`, because `cd` is an external program that changes the directory of the system.
options.why: `cd` is a shell builtin and it only affects the shell that executes it.

options.t: An error, because `cd` cannot be used inside a script.
options.why: It can be used; it just has no effect on the parent shell.

questions.title: Counting the groups
questions.text: For the user `alumno` the command `id -Gn` prints `alumno adm cdrom sudo audio video secops`. What does `id -Gn | wc -w` print?

options.why: `-G` lists all the groups, the primary one included, and `wc -w` counts the 7 words of the line.
The primary group `alumno` is in the list too, so it is not 6.
`wc -w` counts words, not lines: the output is one line but seven words.
There are seven names in the list, not eight.

options.t: A unit file describes a service, a mount point, a timer or another resource that systemd manages.
options.why: True: they are the `.service`, `.mount`, `.timer`... files.

options.t: A target groups units and plays the role that the runlevels had in SysV init.
options.why: True: `multi-user.target` is similar to the old runlevel 3.

options.t: `systemd` uses control groups (cgroups) to keep track of all the processes of a service.
options.why: True: that is how it can stop every process of a service.

options.t: `systemctl isolate multi-user.target` powers the machine off.
options.why: False: it switches to that target, stopping the units that do not belong to it. Powering off is `systemctl poweroff`.

questions.title: Archives and compression
questions.text: Which statement about `tar` and compression is FALSE?

options.t: `tar -cf docs.tar docs` creates an archive without compressing it.
options.why: True: without `z` there is no compression.

options.t: `tar -czf docs.tgz docs` creates a gzip-compressed archive.
options.why: True.

options.t: `tar -tf docs.tar` lists the content of the archive without extracting it.
options.why: True.

options.t: `gzip docs` compresses the directory `docs` into `docs.gz`.
options.why: False: `gzip` compresses files, not directories; it answers "docs is a directory -- ignored". A directory must be packed with `tar` first.

questions.title: A long command on two lines
questions.text: You are typing a long command and want to continue it on the next physical line. What do you do at the end of the first line?

options.t: Type a backslash `\` and press Enter.
options.why: The backslash removes the newline, so the shell reads both lines as one command.

options.t: Type a semicolon `;` and press Enter.
options.why: The semicolon ends the command: the second line would run as a separate command.

options.t: Type a slash `/` and press Enter.
options.why: A slash is just part of the last word.

options.t: Type an ampersand `&` and press Enter.
options.why: `&` runs the first part in the background and then reads a new command.

questions.title: uniq on unsorted data
questions.text: `names` has the lines `b`, `a`, `b`, `c`, `a` (in that order). What happens with `uniq names | wc -l`?

options.t: It prints `5`: `uniq` only collapses equal lines that are adjacent.
options.why: No two equal lines are adjacent here, so nothing is removed.

options.t: It prints `3`, the number of different names.
options.why: That is what `sort names | uniq | wc -l` prints.

options.t: It prints `2`, the number of names that are repeated.
options.why: `uniq` does not count repetitions unless `-c` is used.

options.t: It fails, because `uniq` needs sorted input.
options.why: It accepts any input; it just may not remove all the duplicates.

questions.title: A useless cat
questions.text: Compare `cat f | sort | uniq -c` with `sort f | uniq -c`. Which statement is correct?

options.t: They print the same, but the first starts an extra process (`cat`) that adds nothing.
options.why: `sort` can read the file by itself, so the `cat` only copies the data into the pipe.

options.t: The first one counts the repeated lines and the second does not.
options.why: Both end in `uniq -c`, so both count.

options.t: The second fails, because `sort` cannot read a file given as an argument.
options.why: `sort` reads files given as arguments, and its standard input when there are none.

options.t: The output of the first is sorted and that of the second is not.
options.why: Both pipelines sort before `uniq`.

questions.title: Counting down
questions.text: Which line prints `3`, `2` and `1`, one number per line?

options.t: `i=3; while [ $i -ge 1 ]; do echo $i; i=$((i-1)); done`
options.why: The loop runs while `i` is at least 1 and decrements it each time.

options.t: `i=3; until [ $i -ge 1 ]; do echo $i; i=$((i-1)); done`
options.why: `until` stops as soon as the condition is true, and `3 -ge 1` is true at once: nothing is printed.

options.t: `i=3; while [ $i -le 1 ]; do echo $i; i=$((i-1)); done`
options.why: `3 -le 1` is false at the start, so the body never runs.

options.t: `i=3; while [ $i -ge 1 ]; do echo $i; done`
options.why: `i` never changes, so it prints `3` for ever.

questions.title: The root of the tree and root's home
questions.text: Which statement compares the directories `/` and `/root` correctly?

options.t: `/` is the top of the single directory tree, and `/root` is the home directory of the user `root`.
options.why: Every file of the system is below `/`; `/root` is just one directory in it.

options.t: They are two names for the same directory.
options.why: `/` contains `/root`, `/home`, `/etc` and everything else.

options.t: `/root` is the top of the tree and `/` is the home directory of root.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.t: `/root` is the top of the tree of each user, as `/home` is for the others.
options.why: `/root` is the home of one user; the tree of the whole system has a single top, `/`.

questions.title: Variables and wildcards
questions.text: The current directory has only the files `a` and `b`. What does `name='*'; echo "$name" $name` print?

options.t: `* a b`
options.why: The quoted `"$name"` stays as the text `*`; the unquoted `$name` is expanded to `*` and then the wildcard is expanded to the file names.
The wildcard of the unquoted variable is expanded after the variable: it becomes `a b`.

options.t: `a b a b`
options.why: The quotes stop the expansion of the wildcard in the first word.

options.t: `a b *`
options.why: The order of the two words is `"$name"` first and `$name` second.
